query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack at elevated temperature accelerate degradation by mechanically rupturing the protective oxide/passivation films at phase boundaries, which exposes dissimilar regions that then form localized galvanic cells, thereby enhancing both wear and corrosion rates beyond their isolated effects.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, thermally stabilized multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct phases that are initially protected by continuous oxide/passivation films.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive exposure (using a chloride-based medium) at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (service-relevant conditions), a specified aggressive chloride-containing solution, and controlled mechanical wear parameters that replicate real service loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between dissimilar constituent phases where local differences in composition create galvanic potential differences once the protective oxide film is disrupted.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear ruptures the inherent protective oxide/passivation layer on the alloy surface, especially at phase boundaries. This disruption exposes dissimilar phases that naturally form galvanic cells due to intrinsic potential differences, leading to an accelerated localized corrosion reaction. The enhanced corrosion further degrades the oxide layer and exacerbates mechanical wear, establishing a feedback loop that accelerates the total degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: When exposed simultaneously to wear and corrosion, the overall degradation (both increased material loss from wear and elevated localized corrosion rates) will be significantly higher than the sum of the degradation observed under separate wear-only or corrosion-only conditions. Specifically, there will be a notable increase in corrosion at the phase boundaries along with a higher wear rate due to the loss of oxide protection.
generation.baseline: Comparable tests where the alloy is subjected solely to mechanical wear or solely to corrosive exposure under identical temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions characterized by elevated temperatures, a chloride-rich corrosive medium, and defined mechanical loads. It is expected to operate only when both stressors act concurrently to disrupt the protective oxide layer at the alloy's phase boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative amplification of degradation due to the synergistic effect (i.e., how much more the rates increase relative to baseline) is uncertain and likely depends on the extent of oxide film disruption and the intrinsic potential differences between phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identically processed eutectic high-entropy alloy samples and expose them to three distinct conditions: (a) pure mechanical wear at elevated temperature, (b) isolated corrosive exposure in a chloride-based medium at the same temperature, and (c) simultaneous wear and corrosion. Utilize in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and high-speed imaging to monitor the integrity of the oxide film and the development of local galvanic potentials at phase boundaries.
measurements: Wear volume loss (via profilometry or weight loss analysis)
Electrochemical impedance data (to assess passivation film resistance)
High-speed imaging metrics of oxide film rupture at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under the simultaneous wear and corrosion condition, the total degradation rate (combining wear loss and corrosion current density) is not significantly greater than the sum of the individual effects from the wear-only and corrosion-only tests, or if there is no observable evidence of oxide film rupture and resultant localized galvanic activity at phase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

In the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating, the potential difference between the Mo-depleted FCC phase and the Mo-enriched σ phase created localized galvanic cells. This potential gradient accelerated the oxidation of Co/Fe in the FCC phase region, and the oxide film formed by Co/Fe could not effectively protect the coating, dissolving during the corrosion process. In addition, this potential difference facilitated the transfer of electrons at the phase boundaries, accelerating the selective dissolution of the coating. The presence of Mo and Cr elements in the alloy, particularly their role in passive film formation, was of significant importance []. Cr was especially recognized as a crucial component for corrosion resistance due to its ability to form a stable Cr2O3 oxide layer. This oxide layer effectively prevented direct contact between corrosive media and the alloy matrix, thereby enhancing the overall corrosion resistance. However, the passive film underwent localized breakdown under pitting attack, exposing the underlying material and compromising its protective capability. frame.system: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy in its as-cast, thermally stabilized, multi-phase microstructure, which under service conditions is simultaneously exposed to mechanical wear and corrosive environments at elevated temperatures.
frame.goal: Develop a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains why the alloy experiences accelerated degradation when subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion, including a breakdown into predicted individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a baseline condition.
frame.limitation: Current research lacks a unified explanation of how and why the coupling of wear and corrosion processes leads to an accelerated degradation rate in these complex multi-phase systems.
constraints: The hypothesis must be mechanistic and singular in nature.
It must be accompanied by a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation from alternative models.
Predictions should include changes in total degradation and in the breakdown between wear and corrosion responses relative to a defined, matched baseline alloy.
The explanation must define the boundary conditions relevant to the degradation process.
Supporting evidence should be identified and must include a clear criterion for falsification.
frame.regime: Simulated service conditions at elevated temperatures where both mechanical wear (due to friction and contact stresses) and corrosion (accelerated by high thermal activation of electrochemical reactions) occur concurrently.
prior_attempts: Many studies have independently characterized wear under mechanical load or corrosion under static immersion, but these approaches failed to capture the synergy when both processes act simultaneously.

Prior experimental setups often did not employ a controlled comparative approach to decouple the individual contributions of corrosion and wear, leading to ambiguous interpretations about their accelerated coupling.

decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys largely focused on quantifying wear and corrosion separately, with initial studies using traditional mechanical tests and static corrosion immersion. In subsequent investigations (e.g., studies on laser‐cladded HEA coatings and refractory HEAs), researchers began to notice that the dual‐phase microstructures fostered localized oxide film formation and galvanic interactions between dissimilar phases. Such experiments highlighted how the rupture of a protective film under mechanical action might expose vulnerable phase boundaries to aggressive electrochemical reactions—a trend that indicated a coupling of the mechanisms but did not offer a controlled decoupling to isolate the effects.
decision.unsolved: A unified, mechanistic explanation that causally links wear‐induced disruption of passivating oxide films with enhanced localized galvanic corrosion at the phase boundaries of multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys under elevated temperatures remains unproven. In particular, how the coupling changes the individual contributions of wear and corrosion compared to the baseline (isolated environments) is yet to be established.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled in-situ experimental study that subjects as-cast, thermally stabilized, eutectic high-entropy alloy samples to three test conditions: (a) pure mechanical wear at elevated temperature, (b) pure corrosive exposure under identical thermal conditions, and (c) simultaneous wear and corrosion. Crucially, real-time monitoring (e.g., using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and high-speed imaging of oxide film evolution) should be employed to assess oxide/passivation film integrity and to measure galvanic potential differences at the phase boundaries.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend from isolated to coupled degradation studies. By decoupling and then recombining the effects, it addresses the gap of not yet having a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains how wear disrupts the protective film—triggering localized galvanic corrosion—which in turn accelerates overall degradation. The distinct boundary conditions (elevated temperature, defined corrosive medium, controlled wear parameters) and clear falsification criterion (the absence of a significant increase in corrosion rate and oxide film rupture under combined conditions relative to the isolated tests) will enable a definitive assessment of the proposed mechanism.
